BOOK_A.title: Costs in Class Proceeding
BOOK_A.commentary:
Costs are discretionary in all suits, even class actions.²
Decisions from other provinces can be
misleading, as often their legislation on costs in class actions is different, even opposite.³
The factors in Rr.10.32 and 10.33 are not naturally exclusive; the reference in R.10.32 includes
R.10.33’s factors. And R.10.33 on reducing costs can be inﬂuenced by R.10.32 factors, on “any
other matter related”.⁴
Which factor in Rr.10.32 and 10.33 to use in an individual case, is up to the
trial judge, even in a failed class action.⁵
For costs, access to justice is relevant and disabled elderly people can be a “disadvantaged
group”.⁶
In a class actions costs, what relation the elderly disabled had with their counsel and how
it was funded, are relevant.⁷
Behavior modiﬁcation is a legitimate consideration for party-party costs, especially in a class
action.⁸
That the suit is a class action is itself also relevant.⁹
Deep pockets are generally irrelevant,
but have some weight in a class action.¹⁰

It took years of litigation, in ﬁve provinces, with appeals and objections by large commercial
companies advancing their own common interests, not any public interest, to get approval to
settle class actions, for over $45 million. So three times Column 5 was awarded as costs for that
approval process.¹

footnotes.text: Kerr v. Danier Leather 2007 SCC 44, [2007] 3 SCR 331.

Macaronies Hair Club &c. v. BofA Can. Bank (#_) 2022 ABQB 143, 36 Alta LR(7th) 354 (¶’s 12-13). Even if a provincial statute bars costs of a failed class action, that does not bind the Supreme Court of Canada, and it can award costs to the defendants of a failed Supreme Court of Canada appeal: Sharbern Hldg. v. Vancouver Airport Centre 2011 SCC 23, 416 NR 1.
Elder Advocates of Alta. Socy. v. Alta. Health Serv. (#__) 2021 ABCA 67, 21 Alta LR(7th) 128 (¶ 24).
Elder Advocates v. Alta. Health (#__), supra (¶ 25).
Elder Advocates v. Alta. Health (#__), supra (¶ 37).
Elder Advocates v. Alta. Health (#__), supra (¶ 40).

BOOK_B.title: Costs in class proceeding

commentary.text: Rule 10.32 See Alberta Rules of Court, Alta. Reg. 124/2010, r. 10.32. In Andriuk v. Merrill Lynch Canada Inc., 2014 ABQB 28, 2014 CarswellAlta 61, 578 A.R. 85, 60 C.P.C. (7th) 437, Madam Justice Martin discussed the approach to follow when considering an award of costs in class proceedings. She said, at paragraphs 1, 3, and 4: 1 S.L. MARTIN J.:—This judgment concerns one issue: should the court exercise its discretion to award a multiplier on the costs the plaintiffs agreed to pay after their application to have their claim certified as a class action was dismissed. Alberta is one of a few jurisdictions in Canada that permits costs awards in class proceedings. Nevertheless, any award remains in the discretion of the court, in accordance with the Rules of Court. It is possible that costs will not always follow the event when an application for certification is dismissed because of the underlying goals of class proceedings: the aggregation of claims to pursue efficiency, access to justice and behaviour modification. … 3 Courts have the discretion to award enhanced costs. According to Morrison Petroleum Ltd. v. Phoenix Canada Ltd. (1998), 236 AR 95 some relevant factors to consider when addressing claimed increases to the tariffs include: the difficulty and complexity of the issues; the importance of the case between the parties and or the community at large; the length of the trial; the position and relationship of the parties and their conduct prior to and during the course of the trial; and other factors which may affect the fairness of a cost award. Such factors may have some bearing in a class proceeding. See also Eaton v. HMS Financial Inc., 2010 ABQB 364. 4 The defendants claim that a multiplier is justified based on the difficult and complex issues in this case, the conduct of the litigation, and the resulting length of the application. It is to be remembered that an application for certification as a class action is a preliminary and interlocutory step governed by legislation. If certification is denied, the action proceeds as an individual action, based upon the filed statement of claim. The certification process adds another step in the litigation and involves a multi-part statutory test. To some extent, the mere framework of class proceedings adds difficulty and complexity to any litigation. However, in my view it is not appropriate to conclude that enhanced costs should apply automatically to certification proceedings. The factor of the difficulty and complexity of the issues ought to be gauged by reference to other certification applications. In the end, Madam Justice Martin concluded that in the case before her: 6 However, based on the other factors I have concluded that no multiplier is justified in the circumstances. The complexity and delay are dealt with by allowing recovery for each step in fact taken and the missing elements led to the dismissal of the application. This matter is of significance to the plaintiffs and the larger investor community. Each party has argued the misconduct of the other and case law supports the use of multipliers to discourage behaviours that increase the duration and expense of litigation. However, while the application took some time to be heard and was hard-fought at all stages, I am not prepared to say that that any impugned conduct is sufficient to warrant enhanced costs. 7 Other factors to be considered in relation to the fairness of enhanced costs include the fact that no multiplier was requested or granted in relation to the two previous costs awards in this case: one in favor of each party. Further, a court should consider whether significantly enhanced costs at the preliminary stage may have a disproportionately negative impact on the progress of a filed action. 8 For these reasons no multiplier is granted …. For an example of Rule 10.32 being applied, see: Elder Advocates of Alberta Society v. Alberta, 2020 ABQB 54, 2020 CarswellAlta 96, 96 C.C.L.I. (5th) 236; appeal dismissed 2021 ABCA 67.
